title: Lists, Tuples, Dicts & Sets
tagline: The big four collections in depth: indexing, slicing, unpacking, comprehensions.

lessons.title: Lists: Your ArrayList
lessons.body:
# Lists: Your ArrayList

Lists are ordered, mutable sequences — the workhorse collection:

```python
scores = [85, 92, 78]
scores.append(95)       # [85, 92, 78, 95]
scores[0] = 86          # lists are mutable
print(len(scores))      # 4
```

## Indexing and slicing

Indexing starts at 0; negative indices count from the end. Slices copy a sub-range with `[start:stop:step]`:

```python
items = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(items[0])      # 'a'
print(items[-1])     # 'e' -- last element
print(items[1:3])    # ['b', 'c'] -- stop is EXCLUSIVE
print(items[:2])     # ['a', 'b']
print(items[::2])    # ['a', 'c', 'e'] -- every other
print(items[::-1])   # ['e', 'd', 'c', 'b', 'a'] -- reversed copy
```

The exclusive stop is the #1 slicing bug source: `items[1:3]` has 2 elements, not 3. Think of indices as pointing *between* elements.

## Essential list methods

```python
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums.append(4)        # add ONE item to the end
nums.extend([5, 6])   # add MANY items (vs append([5, 6]), which nests!)
nums.insert(0, 0)     # insert at position
nums.remove(1)        # remove first occurrence of VALUE 1
popped = nums.pop()   # remove and RETURN last item
nums.sort()           # sort in place
print(3 in nums)      # True -- membership test
```

`append` vs `extend` is a classic bug: `append([5, 6])` nests the list as one element; `extend([5, 6])` adds the two items flat. And `sort()` sorts in place and returns `None` — assign the result and you've just thrown your list away.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: a list is `ArrayList` without the generics — `List<String>` becomes just a list, and it happily holds mixed types (don't, but it can). Indexing `items[0]` replaces `items.get(0)`, `len()` replaces `.size()`, and slicing `items[1:3]` replaces `items.subList(1, 3)`. Note `sort()` sorts in place like `Collections.sort()`; the non-mutating version is the `sorted()` builtin. JavaScript comparison: lists are Arrays with different method names — `append` is `push`, `extend` is `push(...items)` or `concat`. Negative indexing `items[-1]` has no JS equivalent (modern JS has `at(-1)`).
keyPoints: Lists are ordered and mutable — `append`, `insert`, `remove`, `pop`, `sort`
Negative indices count from the end; slices use an exclusive stop: `[start:stop]`
`append` adds one item; `extend` adds many — don't confuse them
`sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`; `sorted()` returns a new list

lessons.title: Tuples: Immutable Sequences
lessons.body:
# Tuples: Immutable Sequences

A tuple is an immutable, ordered sequence — a list you can't change:

```python
point = (10, 20)
print(point[0])   # 10 -- indexing works
# point[0] = 5   -- TypeError: tuples don't support item assignment
```

Parentheses are optional; the **comma** makes the tuple:

```python
pair = 1, 2       # this IS a tuple
single = (5,)     # one-element tuple needs the trailing comma!
not_a_tuple = (5)  # just the int 5 in parentheses
```

`(5)` vs `(5,)` is a genuine gotcha — the trailing comma is load-bearing.

## Unpacking

Tuples (and lists) unpack into names — this is how multi-value returns work:

```python
x, y = (10, 20)              # x=10, y=20
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]  # first=1, rest=[2, 3, 4]
a, b = b, a                   # swap with no temp variable
```

The counts must match (unless you use `*`), or you get a `ValueError`.

## When to use a tuple

Use tuples for fixed-shape data: coordinates, RGB colors, dict keys, anything where the *position* has meaning and the contents shouldn't change. If you're appending or removing, you want a list. Tuples are also hashable (when their contents are), so they can be dict keys — lists can't.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: there's no direct tuple type — the closest analogies are a small immutable class or a `record` (Java 16+), but tuples need no declaration at all. Unpacking `x, y = point` has no Java equivalent; you'd write `int x = point.x(); int y = point.y();`. JavaScript comparison: no tuples either — destructuring `const [x, y] = [10, 20]` is the direct equivalent of unpacking, and the swap `a, b = b, a` mirrors `[a, b] = [b, a]`.
keyPoints: Tuples are immutable sequences; the comma (not the parens) makes them
`(5,)` is a tuple; `(5)` is just an int — the trailing comma matters
Unpacking assigns multiple names at once: `x, y = point`
Use tuples for fixed-shape data and dict keys; lists for growing/shrinking collections

lessons.title: Dicts: Your HashMap
lessons.body:
# Dicts: Your HashMap

Dicts map hashable keys to values — the single most-used collection in Python:

```python
user = {"name": "Raymond", "role": "engineer"}
print(user["name"])       # Raymond
user["level"] = "L4"      # add or overwrite
print(user.get("team"))    # None -- no KeyError!
```

## `[]` vs `.get()`

`user["missing"]` raises `KeyError`. `user.get("missing")` returns `None` (or a default you pass: `.get("missing", "n/a")`). Rule of thumb: use `[]` when the key *must* exist (a missing key is a bug worth crashing on), `.get()` when absence is normal.

```python
config = {"retries": 3}
retries = config.get("timeout", 30)  # 30 -- default when absent
```

## Iterating dicts

```python
user = {"name": "Raymond", "role": "engineer"}

for key in user:                 # iterates KEYS
    print(key)

for key, value in user.items():  # the workhorse pattern
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

print("name" in user)           # True -- `in` checks KEYS
print(list(user.keys()))
print(list(user.values()))
```

`in` on a dict checks keys, not values — and it's O(1), which is why dicts (and sets) are the answer to "is X in this collection?" performance questions.

## Keys must be hashable

Strings, numbers, and tuples of hashables work as keys. Lists and dicts don't (they're mutable):

```python
valid = {(10, 20): "point"}  # tuple key: fine
# invalid = {[1, 2]: "x"}   # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: a dict is `HashMap` with literal syntax — `{"a": 1}` instead of `new HashMap<>()` plus `put` calls, and `user["name"]` instead of `user.get("name")`. Note the inversion: Python's `.get()` is the *safe* accessor (returns `None`), while Java's `.get()` is the one that returns null on missing keys. Iteration via `.items()` mirrors `entrySet()`. JavaScript comparison: dicts are what you wish plain objects were — a real hash map where keys can be any hashable type, not just strings. For JS `Map` users: `d[k]`, `.get(k)`, `k in d`, and `.items()` map to `m.get(k)`, `m.get(k)`, `m.has(k)`, and `m.entries()` — with nicer syntax.
keyPoints: Dicts map hashable keys to values: `{"name": "Raymond"}`
`d[key]` raises `KeyError` on missing keys; `d.get(key, default)` doesn't
`for k, v in d.items()` is the standard iteration pattern
`in` checks keys in O(1); keys must be hashable (no lists/dicts as keys)

lessons.title: Sets: Unique Collections and Fast Membership
lessons.body:
# Sets: Unique Collections and Fast Membership

A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items:

```python
tags = {"python", "backend", "python"}
print(tags)          # {'backend', 'python'} -- duplicate gone, order not guaranteed
tags.add("api")
tags.discard("zzz")  # no error even though 'zzz' isn't there
```

Use `discard`, not `remove`, unless you *want* a `KeyError` on missing items — `discard` is the forgiving one.

## Set operations

```python
a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {3, 4, 5}
print(a | b)  # {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} -- union
print(a & b)  # {3}             -- intersection
print(a - b)  # {1, 2}          -- difference
print(a ^ b)  # {1, 2, 4, 5}    -- symmetric difference
```

These read beautifully for real problems: "users in both groups" is `group_a & group_b`.

## The real reason sets exist: O(1) membership

Checking `x in some_list` scans the whole list — O(n). Checking `x in some_set` hashes — O(1):

```python
# slow for large data
if user_id in user_id_list:
    print("found")
```

```python
# fast: convert once, test many times
user_id_set = set(user_id_list)
if user_id in user_id_set:
    print("found")
```

Any time you're doing repeated membership tests against a large collection, reach for a set. Also note: `{}` is an empty **dict**, not a set — write `set()` for an empty set.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: a set is `HashSet` with literal syntax and operator overloads — `a & b` instead of `retainAll` gymnastics, `a | b` instead of `addAll`. The `{}`-is-a-dict gotcha has no Java parallel; just memorize `set()` for empty. JavaScript comparison: nearly identical to JS `Set` — `add`/`discard` (like `delete`), `|`/`&` have no operator form in JS (you'd spread and filter), and the O(1) membership argument is the same reason you'd pick a JS `Set` over an array for lookups.
keyPoints: Sets hold unique, unordered, hashable items; `{}` is a dict — use `set()` for empty
`|` union, `&` intersection, `-` difference, `^` symmetric difference
Membership tests are O(1) — convert lists to sets for repeated lookups
`discard` won't error on missing items; `remove` will

lessons.title: Comprehensions and Picking the Right Structure
lessons.body:
# Comprehensions and Picking the Right Structure

Comprehensions build collections in one expressive line:

```python
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]
evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
```

Read them left to right: "square each x, for x in range(10), keeping only evens." Every comprehension has an expression, a loop, and an optional condition:

```python
# list: [expr for x in items if cond]
# set:  {expr for x in items if cond}
# dict: {key: value for x in items if cond}

names = ["amy", "bob", "cara"]
upper_set = {n.upper() for n in names}       # {'AMY', 'BOB', 'CARA'}
lengths = {n: len(n) for n in names}         # {'amy': 3, 'bob': 3, 'cara': 4}
```

Comprehensions aren't just shorter — they're faster than equivalent `append` loops, and they're the idiom every Python codebase expects.

## Generator expressions: lazy comprehensions

Parentheses instead of brackets give you a lazy, one-shot iterator — values are produced on demand, never stored:

```python
total = sum(x ** 2 for x in range(10_000_000))  # no giant list in memory
```

If you're only iterating once (summing, joining, passing to a function), the generator form avoids building a list you immediately throw away.

## Choosing the right structure

- **List:** ordered, mutable, duplicates OK — the default sequence.
- **Tuple:** fixed shape, immutable — coordinates, records, dict keys.
- **Dict:** key to value lookup — configs, indexes, caches.
- **Set:** uniqueness + fast membership — deduping, "is X in the group?"

When in doubt, start with a list or dict. Reach for tuples when shape is fixed, sets when uniqueness or lookup speed matters.
lessons.jsNote: Java comparison: comprehensions are Java Streams without the ceremony — `[x*2 for x in items]` is `items.stream().map(x -> x*2).collect(toList())` in a fraction of the characters. Generator expressions are lazy like streams, but simpler. JavaScript comparison: list comprehensions are `map`+`filter` fused — `[x**2 for x in nums if x > 0]` is `nums.filter(x => x > 0).map(x => x**2)`. Dict comprehensions are `Object.fromEntries(nums.map(...))` without the awkwardness. Once comprehensions click, you'll miss them in every other language.
keyPoints: Comprehensions: `[expr for x in items if cond]` — also work for sets and dicts
They're faster and more idiomatic than append-loops
Generator expressions `(expr for x in items)` are lazy — no list built
List = default sequence; tuple = fixed shape; dict = lookup; set = uniqueness/membership

exercises.title: First and Last
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `first_and_last(items)` that returns a tuple `(first, last)` of the first and last elements of a list.

Example calls:

```python
first_and_last([10, 20, 30, 40])
# returns: (10, 40)
```
hints: Negative index `-1` is the last element
Separate two return values with a comma to return a tuple

exercises.title: Word Lengths
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `word_lengths(words)` that returns a dict mapping each word to its length.

Example calls:

```python
word_lengths(["hi", "hello", "hey"])
# returns: {"hi": 2, "hello": 5, "hey": 3}
```
exercises.solution:
def word_lengths(words):
    return {word: len(word) for word in words}
hints: A dict comprehension builds this in one line

exercises.title: Even Squares
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `even_squares(n)` that returns a list of the squares of even numbers from 0 up to (but not including) `n`, using a single list comprehension.

Example calls:

```python
even_squares(10)
# returns: [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]
```
exercises.solution:
def even_squares(n):
    return [x ** 2 for x in range(n) if x % 2 == 0]
hints: Structure: `[expression for x in range(n) if condition]`

exercises.title: Common Ground
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `common_items(a, b)` that returns a **set** of items appearing in both lists.

Example calls:

```python
common_items([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4])
# returns: {2, 3}
```
exercises.solution:
def common_items(a, b):
    return set(a) & set(b)
hints: Convert both lists to sets first

exercises.title: Vote Tally
exercises.prompt:
Write a function `tally_votes(votes)` that takes a list of vote strings and returns a dict mapping each candidate to their vote count.

Example calls:

```python
tally_votes(["amy", "bob", "amy", "amy", "cara", "bob"])
# returns: {"amy": 3, "bob": 2, "cara": 1}
```
hints: This counting pattern is so common it has a stdlib shortcut: `collections.Counter`
